screens.title: Ansible Roles — structure and purpose
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible Roles are a convention for organizing playbook content into reusable units that contain tasks, handlers, templates, variables, and metadata. A role packages a logical piece of automation — for example, router_base_config — so you avoid a single monolithic playbook that is hard to maintain. Roles define a clear directory structure that Ansible expects. This structure helps teams find where to add a handler, where templates live, and where default and override variables are stored. For instance, a typical role includes tasks/main. yml, handlers/main. yml, templates/, vars/main. yml, defaults/main. yml, and meta/main. yml. When you call a role from a playbook, Ansible loads those paths automatically so the role behaves like a mini-playbook with its own scope. A common misconception is that roles are only for very large projects; in truth, even small automation benefits from logical separation because testing, versioning, and reuse scale better. Example: create separate roles for base router config, interface configuration, and OSPF so changes to one area don't require editing unrelated tasks. Takeaway: roles make code easier to read, test, and share across teams. Ansible Roles — structure and purpose means use roles to group related tasks and assets so your automation becomes maintainable and shareable.. In practical terms, why roles organize automation and how a role directory looks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Roles — structure
Role directory example
roles/
  router_base_config/
    tasks/
      main.yml
    handlers/
      main.yml
    templates/
      ntp.j2
    vars/
      main.yml
    defaults/
      main.yml
    meta/
      main.yml
This directory layout is standard. Tasks define the work, handlers react to notifications, templates hold Jinja2 files, vars and defaults set values, and meta can declare dependencies. Roles are applied in a playbook using the roles: list.
Why roles matter
  • Promote code reuse: one role can be applied to many hosts with different variables.
  • Reduce merge conflicts: teams edit role internals rather than a large playbook.
  • Make testing easier: test a role independently in a lab before applying.
Example
Create a router_base_config role to set hostname, NTP, and common security settings once, then reuse it for each router type.
Key Takeaway

Treat each role as a focused feature; keep roles small and composable for maximum reuse.

screens.title: Applying roles from a playbook
screens.narratorSegment: Calling roles from a playbook is straightforward but important to get right. A playbook lists hosts, connection type, privilege escalation, and then a roles: list. Roles inherit the playbook context but keep their own scoped files, making it easy to pass or override variables. For example, a play that targets cisco_routers can include vars_files to bring in vault-encrypted secrets, then list router_base_config under roles. The role will run its tasks/main. yml and any handlers it notifies. One practical pattern is to include host-specific variables in host_vars while keeping defaults in defaults/main. yml within the role. This enables safe overrides without editing role internals. A common misconception is that roles isolate variables completely; in fact, variable precedence still applies, so you must understand where a value originates. Example playbook snippet shows connection: network_cli, become_method: enable, and a vars_files reference for vault. yml. When you run the playbook, consider running with --check first to preview changes and avoid accidental outages. Question: which level should hold a password used by multiple hosts? Put shared secrets in an encrypted vars file rather than inside a role defaults.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Call roles
Playbook example
---
- name: Apply base configuration to routers
  hosts: cisco_routers
  connection: network_cli
  become: true
  become_method: enable
  vars_files:
    - vault.yml

  roles:
    - router_base_config
This playbook uses a role to apply the base config. The role's tasks and templates run as if they were inline, but are kept in a separate folder for clarity.
Practical notes
  • Place secrets in vars_files and encrypt with Vault rather than hard-coding into roles.
  • Use defaults/main.yml for safe defaults and vars/main.yml for role-specific hard settings.
  • Run --check to preview role changes on devices without making modifications.
Misconception
Roles are not a security boundary; they follow Ansible's variable precedence, so encrypt shared secrets and avoid storing plain passwords in repository files.

screens.title: Jinja2 Templating Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Jinja2 is the templating engine Ansible uses to render files with variables and logic. Instead of hardcoding configuration, you build a template that includes placeholders and control structures. When the template is rendered, Ansible substitutes variable values and evaluates loops and conditionals, producing a final config file ready to apply. An important example from the chapter shows an OSPF template using a process id variable and a for loop over networks. This approach lets one template serve many devices. For instance, the template includes a for loop that iterates over an ospf_networks list and emits network statements for each item. A common beginner mistake is to attempt complex device-side templating; render templates on the control node when device Jinja support is limited. Also ensure variables referenced in templates exist or provide defaults to avoid runtime errors. The core idea: treat templates as parameterized blueprints for configuration, and use loops and conditionals to express repetition and optional blocks safely. Jinja2 Templating Basics means write jinja2 templates that accept variables and produce final configuration for many devices without modifying the template itself.. In practical terms, use templates to generate device-specific configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Jinja2 Template
Example template (ospf.j2)
router ospf {{ ospf_process_id }}
{% for network in ospf_networks %}
  network {{ network.address }} {{ network.wildcard }} area {{ network.area }}
{% endfor %}
When rendered with ospf_process_id and an ospf_networks list, this template emits one network line per list item. Use filters if you need formatting or conditional blocks for optional features.
Template best practices
  • Provide sensible defaults to avoid missing variable errors.
  • Keep templates readable: prefer small loops over nested complex logic.
  • Render on the control node with delegate_to: localhost when possible.
Concrete example
A single ospf.j2 file can create distinct OSPF configs for dozens of routers by feeding it the right network lists per host.

screens.title: Render and Apply Templates
screens.narratorSegment: Rendering a template and applying it safely is a two-step pattern frequently used for network devices. First, use ansible. builtin. template to render the Jinja2 file on the control node by adding delegate_to: localhost. This avoids limitations of device modules and lets the control node evaluate filters or lookups. The task writes the rendered configuration to a temporary file, typically under /tmp. After rendering, call a config module such as cisco. ios. ios_config and point the src parameter at the temporary file to apply changes to the device. Finally, clean up the temporary file on the control node. This process prevents accidental device-side template evaluation and centralizes rendering logic. A concrete example in the chapter shows rendering to /tmp/ospf_config. txt and then using cisco. ios. ios_config to apply it. Remember to notify handlers, like a Save Configuration handler, so device-specific save logic runs when appropriate. Misconception: rendering locally doesn't bypass device validation; always validate with --check and a lab before production runs. Render and Apply Templates means render jinja2 templates on the control node and then apply the rendered file to devices for predictable automation.. In practical terms, template rendering with delegate_to and applying rendered config. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Template render & apply
Render template task
- name: Configure OSPF using template
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: ospf.j2
    dest: /tmp/ospf_config.txt
  delegate_to: localhost
  vars:
    ospf_process_id: 1
    ospf_networks:
      - { address: "10.0.0.0", wildcard: "0.0.0.255", area: 0 }
      - { address: "10.0.1.0", wildcard: "0.0.0.255", area: 0 }
This writes a rendered file on the control node. Use template variables or host facts for per-device content.
Apply and cleanup
- name: Apply OSPF config to device
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    src: /tmp/ospf_config.txt
  notify: Save Configuration

- name: Remove temporary file
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: /tmp/ospf_config.txt
    state: absent
  delegate_to: localhost
Apply rendered config, trigger handlers to save, and then remove temporary artifacts to keep the control node tidy.

screens.title: Variables and Facts
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible variables are the inputs that make templates and tasks dynamic. They can be defined in inventory, host_vars, group_vars, roles (vars and defaults), playbooks, or passed on the command line. Facts are special variables gathered automatically from managed hosts when gather_facts is true; they include hostnames, interfaces, OS versions, and IP addresses. You can reference facts like ansible_facts['hostname'] in templates or tasks to inject discovered data into configuration. Understand variable precedence to predict which value wins when the same name exists in multiple places. For example, a host_vars file overrides group_vars and role defaults. Practical tip: use defaults/main. yml in a role for safe fallback values and avoid relying on variables that may not exist. A common error is assuming a fact exists; always guard templates or tasks with conditionals or default filters. Example: use an interface list variable defined in a role to render per-interface configuration. Proper variable management reduces duplication and prevents surprises when deploying to devices with different capabilities. Variables and Facts means define variables at the appropriate level and use facts to incorporate discovered device properties safely.. In practical terms, where variables come from and how to use gathered facts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Variable sources
  • Inventory and host_vars/group_vars
  • Role defaults and vars
  • Playbook vars, vars_files, and command-line overrides
Remember precedence: a variable set at a higher precedence level overrides lower ones. Use role defaults for safe fallbacks.
Using facts
Facts provide discovered data. Example usage in a template: {{ ansible_facts['hostname'] }}. Guard against missing facts with defaults or conditionals.
Practical example

screens.title: Loops and Conditionals
screens.narratorSegment: Loops and conditionals let you express repetition and selective execution in playbooks. Use the loop keyword to iterate over a list or dictionary and perform the same task for each item. For example, configuring multiple interfaces can be done with a loop that supplies name and description for each interface. Conditionals run tasks only when a condition holds by using when. Combine them to ensure work only runs for matching items. The chapter shows a loop example where two interface objects are looped and a when condition ensures a task runs only for GigabitEthernet1/0/1. A subtle pitfall is using when with looped items; reference the loop item correctly to avoid unexpected skips. Another common mistake is relying on unstructured output from modules in a when clause; use registered variables and debug to inspect values before gating behavior. Concrete pattern: loop over interfaces, set state or description depending on a property, and use failed_when to detect and handle unexpected results. This makes playbooks more resilient and adaptable across diverse hardware. Loops and Conditionals means use loop to iterate over items and when to conditionally execute tasks so playbooks are concise and adaptive.. In practical terms, repeat work safely and run tasks only when needed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This makes playbooks more resilient and adaptable across diverse hardware. keyIdea.text: Use loop to iterate over items and when to conditionally execute tasks so playbooks are concise and adaptive.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Loops & Conditionals
Loop example
- name: Configure interface description if interface is GigE1/0/1
  cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
    config:
      - name: "{{ item.name }}"
        description: "{{ item.description }}"
    state: merged
  loop:
    - { name: "GigabitEthernet1/0/1", description: "Primary Uplink" }
    - { name: "GigabitEthernet1/0/2", description: "Secondary Uplink" }
  when: item.name == "GigabitEthernet1/0/1"
This pattern configures multiple interfaces but applies the description only to the specific interface that matches the condition.
Best practices
  • Inspect item structure with debug before using it in complex conditionals.
  • Prefer simple comparisons in when clauses to reduce logic bugs.
  • Use loop_control to label iterations for clearer logging when needed.
Common mistake
Assuming item attributes always exist. Add defensive checks or defaults to avoid runtime failures in loops.

screens.title: Ansible Vault — secure sensitive data
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible Vault is the tool you use to encrypt sensitive files like passwords, A P I keys, and private keys so they are not stored in plain text. You can encrypt a single file or multiple files and edit them securely with ansible-vault edit. When running playbooks that need Vault secrets, you supply a vault password interactively or via a password file, for example with --vault-password-file. Commands in the chapter show how to encrypt vars/vault. yml and edit it securely. A practical habit is to keep encrypted secrets in a vars_files entry in your playbook so the role reads them at runtime. Never commit unencrypted secrets to your repository. A misconception is that Vault replaces system secrets management; Vault secures Ansible content but teams should still use centralized secret management for cross-system policies. Example: encrypt the file that holds device enable passwords and then reference that file in vars_files so playbooks can access the encrypted values at execution time without exposing them in source control. Ansible Vault — secure sensitive data means encrypt variables and files with ansible vault and load them at runtime to prevent exposing sensitive data in your repository.. In practical terms, encrypt variable files and manage secrets safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Common Vault commands

ansible-vault edit vars/vault.yml
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini playbook.yml --ask-vault-pass

screens.title: Error Handling and Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: Robust playbooks must handle errors gracefully and provide diagnostic output when issues occur. Two useful features are ignore_errors and failed_when. ignore_errors: true lets a specific task fail without stopping the whole playbook, which is useful when a non-critical change might fail on some devices. failed_when allows you to define custom failure criteria based on module output so you can mark a task as successful even if a module reports unusual output, or conversely treat subtle conditions as failures. The debug module is essential for printing variable values or registered outputs during development and troubleshooting. Run ansible-playbook with increased verbosity, for example -vvv, to see task-level details and module JSON. A common misconception is to blanket ignore all errors; this hides real problems. Instead, use ignore_errors sparingly and pair it with debug tasks that log context. Example pattern from the chapter shows using ignore_errors on a risky config and then a debug task to print my_variable. Also use --check mode to validate changes before applying them in production. Takeaway: catch and log errors, but don't silence them without recording why. Error Handling and Debugging means use ignore_errors and failed_when with debug output to continue automation where safe and capture context for later remediation.. In practical terms, continue safely and capture useful information when things fail. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Error Handling
Useful patterns
- name: Attempt a risky configuration
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines: "no ip routing"
  ignore_errors: true

- name: Debug variable value
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    var: my_variable
Use debug after an ignored failure to capture context. Register outputs if you need to inspect module return values in conditionals.
Comparison: stop vs continue
Stopping on failures is safe for critical configuration. Continuing is useful for inventory-wide operations where one device's failure shouldn't block others. Choose behavior based on risk and include logging to investigate failures later.
Pro tip
Use -vvv during development and write small tasks that are easy to reason about when failures occur.

screens.title: Lab: Dynamic Interface Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: In the lab you will create an Ansible project that renders interface configuration via a Jinja2 template inside a role and applies it to a Cisco IOS XE device. Start by creating the directory tree: ansible_project with inventory. ini, site. yml, and roles/interface_config containing tasks, templates, and vars. Define interfaces_to_configure in roles/interface_config/vars/main. yml as a list of dictionaries with name, description, and IP fields. Write a template, interface_config. j2, that loops over interfaces_to_configure and emits interface commands. In tasks/main. yml render the template with ansible. builtin. template delegate_to: localhost, write to /tmp/{{ inventory_hostname }}_interface_config. txt, then call cisco. ios. ios_config using that file and notify a handler Save Configuration. Finally remove the temporary file with a delegated file task. Before running against hardware, set ANSIBLE_ENABLE_PASS in the environment and run ansible-playbook with --check to preview changes. After verifying, remove --check and run the playbook for real, then validate with show run commands on the device. This exercise ties together roles, templates, facts, and handlers in a safe workflow. Project structure

screens.title: Safety and Maintainability Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Maintainable automation is also safe automation. Key practices from the chapter include keeping roles small and focused, avoiding hard-coded secrets, and preferring templates over repeated tasks. Store sensitive values in Vault-encrypted files and reference them in vars_files rather than embedding passwords in roles. Use role defaults for sensible fallbacks, and keep host-specific overrides in host_vars so inventory drives per-device differences. Use handlers to save configuration only when a change occurs to minimize unnecessary device writes. During development, run with --check and high verbosity to examine planned changes, and validate on a lab device. For team collaboration, place roles in version control and add clear README files describing variables and expected inputs. A common misconception is that larger roles are easier to manage; in practice, smaller, well-scoped roles make updates safer and reviews simpler. Example: put OSPF logic in its own role so changing OSPF behavior doesn't risk interface configuration logic. Safety and Maintainability Best Practices means adopt small roles, encrypted secrets, dry runs, and clear variable ownership to reduce mistakes and enable safe teamwork.. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Common mistakes when adopting Ansible for networks include rendering templates with missing variables, applying risky commands without dry-run verification, storing credentials in plain text, and misusing variable precedence which leads to unexpected values. A frequent example is running a command that disables a feature like ip routing without testing, which could break connectivity. To recover and debug, run playbooks with -vvv to inspect returned JSON from modules, use ansible. builtin. debug to print registered variables, and apply ignore_errors with caution paired with debug so you capture failure context. If a template fails because a variable is missing, add default filters or guard blocks in the template. For stateful mistakes on devices, use handlers to save known-good configuration and maintain backups before automation runs. A helpful practice is creating a step in your deployment checklist to run --check, review diffs, and then run a limited rollout before full-scale deployment. Always validate in a lab first to learn edge cases of device models and OS versions. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to scale network automation using Ansible's advanced features. We'll focus on structuring automation with roles so content stays modular, using Jinja2 templates to render device-specific configurations, and managing variables and facts so playbooks adapt to each router or switch. You'll also see how to protect secrets with Ansible Vault and how to catch problems early with debug, ignore_errors, and failed_when patterns. These practices prevent fragile playbooks and accidental outages. For example, a single Jinja2 template can generate different OSPF statements for many routers by reading a small list of networks. A role groups tasks, handlers, templates, and defaults so teams can share and reuse the same logic. We will also highlight common mistakes, like applying risky commands without a dry run, and show how to use a lab and the --check option safely.

By the end of this chapter you will organize Ansible projects into roles so automation is reusable and maintainable. That means breaking large playbooks into logical components such as a router base role, an interface role, or an OSPF role, and understanding the directory layout these roles expect. You will also write Jinja2 templates to produce device-specific configuration, using loops and filters to avoid duplication. You'll manage variables and facts so playbooks adapt to each host, and you'll use loops and conditionals to run tasks only when appropriate. Finally, you'll begin using Ansible Vault to protect passwords and keys. A concrete example is creating a template that renders interface statements for two interfaces based on a small list of interface objects. You'll see why modular roles plus templating let the same code manage many devices without manual edits. As you read, consider how each objective reduces manual error and supports team collaboration.

In the hands-on section you'll build a role that renders interface configuration with a Jinja2 template, then applies it to a Cisco IOS XE router. You'll create the role directory layout, declare interfaces as variables, and render a template on the control node before sending it to the device. This teaches practical skills: delegating template rendering to localhost, using facts like the host name inside descriptions, and invoking handlers to save configuration. You will also run the playbook in check mode first and then run it for real, learning how to verify results on the device. A key safety habit is exporting your enable password into an environment variable so it is not hard-coded in files. These applied skills bridge theory to safe real-world automation. Learning Objectives — Applied Skills means by practicing the lab you will combine roles, templates, variables, vault, and dry runs to deploy repeatable, safe configuration to network devices.. In practical terms, concrete skills you'll practice in the lab activity. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ansible Roles are a convention for organizing playbook content into reusable units that contain tasks, handlers, templates, variables, and metadata. A role packages a logical piece of automation — for example, router_base_config — so you avoid a single monolithic playbook that is hard to maintain. Roles define a clear directory structure that Ansible expects. This structure helps teams find where to add a handler, where templates live, and where default and override variables are stored. For instance, a typical role includes tasks/main. yml, handlers/main. yml, templates/, vars/main. yml, defaults/main. yml, and meta/main. yml. When you call a role from a playbook, Ansible loads those paths automatically so the role behaves like a mini-playbook with its own scope. A common misconception is that roles are only for very large projects; in truth, even small automation benefits from logical separation because testing, versioning, and reuse scale better. Example: create separate roles for base router config, interface configuration, and OSPF so changes to one area don't require editing unrelated tasks. Takeaway: roles make code easier to read, test, and share across teams. Ansible Roles — structure and purpose means use roles to group related tasks and assets so your automation becomes maintainable and shareable.. In practical terms, why roles organize automation and how a role directory looks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Calling roles from a playbook is straightforward but important to get right. A playbook lists hosts, connection type, privilege escalation, and then a roles: list. Roles inherit the playbook context but keep their own scoped files, making it easy to pass or override variables. For example, a play that targets cisco_routers can include vars_files to bring in vault-encrypted secrets, then list router_base_config under roles. The role will run its tasks/main. yml and any handlers it notifies. One practical pattern is to include host-specific variables in host_vars while keeping defaults in defaults/main. yml within the role. This enables safe overrides without editing role internals. A common misconception is that roles isolate variables completely; in fact, variable precedence still applies, so you must understand where a value originates. Example playbook snippet shows connection: network_cli, become_method: enable, and a vars_files reference for vault. yml. When you run the playbook, consider running with --check first to preview changes and avoid accidental outages. Question: which level should hold a password used by multiple hosts? Put shared secrets in an encrypted vars file rather than inside a role defaults.

Jinja2 is the templating engine Ansible uses to render files with variables and logic. Instead of hardcoding configuration, you build a template that includes placeholders and control structures. When the template is rendered, Ansible substitutes variable values and evaluates loops and conditionals, producing a final config file ready to apply. An important example from the chapter shows an OSPF template using a process id variable and a for loop over networks. This approach lets one template serve many devices. For instance, the template includes a for loop that iterates over an ospf_networks list and emits network statements for each item. A common beginner mistake is to attempt complex device-side templating; render templates on the control node when device Jinja support is limited. Also ensure variables referenced in templates exist or provide defaults to avoid runtime errors. The core idea: treat templates as parameterized blueprints for configuration, and use loops and conditionals to express repetition and optional blocks safely. Rendering a template and applying it safely is a two-step pattern frequently used for network devices. First, use ansible. builtin. template to render the Jinja2 file on the control node by adding delegate_to: localhost. This avoids limitations of device modules and lets the control node evaluate filters or lookups. The task writes the rendered configuration to a temporary file, typically under /tmp. After rendering, call a config module such as cisco. ios. ios_config and point the src parameter at the temporary file to apply changes to the device. Finally, clean up the temporary file on the control node. This process prevents accidental device-side template evaluation and centralizes rendering logic. A concrete example in the chapter shows rendering to /tmp/ospf_config. txt and then using cisco. ios. ios_config to apply it. Remember to notify handlers, like a Save Configuration handler, so device-specific save logic runs when appropriate. Misconception: rendering locally doesn't bypass device validation; always validate with --check and a lab before production runs. Ansible variables are the inputs that make templates and tasks dynamic. They can be defined in inventory, host_vars, group_vars, roles (vars and defaults), playbooks, or passed on the command line. Facts are special variables gathered automatically from managed hosts when gather_facts is true; they include hostnames, interfaces, OS versions, and IP addresses. You can reference facts like ansible_facts['hostname'] in templates or tasks to inject discovered data into configuration. Understand variable precedence to predict which value wins when the same name exists in multiple places. For example, a host_vars file overrides group_vars and role defaults. Practical tip: use defaults/main. yml in a role for safe fallback values and avoid relying on variables that may not exist. A common error is assuming a fact exists; always guard templates or tasks with conditionals or default filters. Example: use an interface list variable defined in a role to render per-interface configuration. Proper variable management reduces duplication and prevents surprises when deploying to devices with different capabilities. Loops and conditionals let you express repetition and selective execution in playbooks. Use the loop keyword to iterate over a list or dictionary and perform the same task for each item. For example, configuring multiple interfaces can be done with a loop that supplies name and description for each interface. Conditionals run tasks only when a condition holds by using when. Ansible Vault is the tool you use to encrypt sensitive files like passwords, A P I keys, and private keys so they are not stored in plain text. You can encrypt a single file or multiple files and edit them securely with ansible-vault edit. When running playbooks that need Vault secrets, you supply a vault password interactively or via a password file, for example with --vault-password-file. Commands in the chapter show how to encrypt vars/vault. yml and edit it securely. A practical habit is to keep encrypted secrets in a vars_files entry in your playbook so the role reads them at runtime. Never commit unencrypted secrets to your repository. Robust playbooks must handle errors gracefully and provide diagnostic output when issues occur. Two useful features are ignore_errors and failed_when. ignore_errors: true lets a specific task fail without stopping the whole playbook, which is useful when a non-critical change might fail on some devices. failed_when allows you to define custom failure criteria based on module output so you can mark a task as successful even if a module reports unusual output, or conversely treat subtle conditions as failures. The debug module is essential for printing variable values or registered outputs during development and troubleshooting. Run ansible-playbook with increased verbosity, for example -vvv, to see task-level details and module JSON. A common misconception is to blanket ignore all errors; this hides real problems. Instead, use ignore_errors sparingly and pair it with debug tasks that log context. Takeaway: catch and log errors, but don't silence them without recording why. Store sensitive values in Vault-encrypted files and reference them in vars_files rather than embedding passwords in roles. Common mistakes when adopting Ansible for networks include rendering templates with missing variables, applying risky commands without dry-run verification, storing credentials in plain text, and misusing variable precedence which leads to unexpected values. These three concepts are the backbone of advanced Ansible network automation. First, roles encapsulate related automation assets into reusable units. They make playbooks readable, reduce duplication, and simplify testing. Second, Jinja2 templating lets you render device configurations dynamically, using loops and conditionals to express per-device differences in a single template. Third, variable management and facts let playbooks adapt to each host’s properties; place variables at the correct precedence level and use gathered facts to include discovered values like the hostname. Together these ideas enable repeatable, maintainable, and scalable network automation.
